https://www.politico.eu/article/peter-ma.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Thursday cast doubt on a deal struck by his predecessor that would see Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom expand Hungary’s nuclear power capacity. Weeks of extreme heat and drought have pushed the Danube River to record lows , slashing output at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant — which normally supplies around a third of the country’s electricity — to little more than 10 percent . “These plans were accepted despite the fact that nuclear power plants that do not operate with a closed-circuit cooling system and are so exposed to the environment are no longer being built in the world,” said Magyar, per local media . Advertisement Advertisement Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev wrote that the Russian state nuclear company was still on schedule with two new reactors at Paks despite Hungary’s change of government in April , which saw Magyar oust Russia-friendly incumbent Viktor Orbán. Concrete preparation for Unit 5 is more than 80 percent complete, he said, while work on Unit 6 is advancing and reactor components are already being manufactured. “We are ready for dialogue,” Likhachev said, adding that Rosatom had received no questions from Hungary’s new government. Magyar challenged that account hours later. Under the original contract, Paks II should have been operating by 2024, he told reporters in a press conference Thursday. Instead, Hungary has spent roughly 1,000 billion forints (€2.8 billion) on a site he described as little more than depots and “two large concrete pits.” “I don’t really see that they have adhered to the contract,” Magyar said. His government is now carrying out a full review of the project , including its financing and cooling arrangements. The review cuts at one of Orbán’s signature deals with Russia. Orbán struck the Paks II agreement in Moscow in 2014 , handing Rosatom the two-reactor expansion backed by up to €10 billion in Russian state financing. Two years later, he called it the “deal of the century.” Those ties survived Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine . As recently as March this year, Orbán’s foreign minister Péter Szijjártó admitted to discussing EU sanctions with senior Russian officials after leaked calls showed him boasting that a bank linked to Paks had been kept off a sanctions list. Downstream, Romania shut the second and last operating reactor at Cernavodă on Thursday after the Danube fell too low to supply its cooling pumps. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.newsday.com/news/nation/pola.text: Nastya Podorozhnya stands in the kitchen of the shelter which the Martynka non-profit is running in Krakow, Poland, Thursday, July 2, 2026. Credit: AP/Claudia Ciobanu By The Associated Press August 25, 2026 1:04 am Share KRAKOW, Poland — When Nastya Podorozhnya's relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms. Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began. But days before Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she rushed back to Ukraine to help her sister and nieces get out. As she returned to Poland alongside an influx of refugees in the war’s first days, she witnessed the outpouring of support from Polish volunteers. But she also spotted a risk: Ukrainian women accepting help from strangers could become vulnerable to human traffickers. That was when she decided to found Martynka, a helpline and support group for female Ukrainian refugees escaping gender-based violence. Four years later, she is struggling to keep the organization afloat. Funding for refugee support is drying up, hostility toward Ukrainians is growing, and Poland still lacks a long-term integration strategy. As war fatigue deepens, politicians are increasingly exploiting anti-refugee sentiment for political gain. Sign up for the Breaking News newsletter Get the latest breaking news as it happens. By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy . The shift is being felt by groups such as Martynka. While fundraising was relatively easy in the first months of the war, international donors have since turned their attention to other global crises. Martynka's shelter, located in an inconspicuous two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow, has hosted more than 100 women and children. Women receive help to escape abusers and access medical care, psychological support, jobs and housing. Nastya Podorozhnya stands in one of the two bedrooms of the shelter which the Martynka non-profit is running in Krakow, Poland, Thursday, July 2, 2026. Credit: AP/Claudia Ciobanu “It often starts with me having tea in this very kitchen with the women and they tell me what happened to them and I say ‘girl, same,’” Podorozhnya told The Associated Press during an interview in the Krakow shelter, referring to her own experience of a man trying to rape her on a street in Poland in 2016. As Podorozhnya and her colleagues struggle to raise enough money to keep the shelter open, she says calls for donations frequently trigger a torrent of online abuse. “It's because I’m Ukrainian,” she said. Ukrainian refugees contribute to Poland’s economy Around 3.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in the first weeks of the war, according to the U.N. Poles greeted them at train stations and opened their homes to them, while the government granted refugees access to jobs and social security benefits. Refugees fleeing the conflict in neighboring Ukraine arrive to in Przemysl, Poland, Sunday, Feb. 27, 2022. Credit: AP/Petr David Josek The two countries share a long history of brutality at the hands of Russia, and Poland remains a key ally to Ukraine in the war. By the end of 2022, the number of Ukrainian refugees in Poland had stabilized at around 1 million. Those who stayed were rapidly absorbed into the labor market: More than 70% found employment, and a Deloitte study estimated that they contributed 2.7% of Poland’s gross domestic product in 2024. In addition to the refugees, most of whom are women and children, more than 1 million Ukrainians were already living in Poland before the war, primarily as economic migrants. Historical grievances resurface The refugees have increasingly become targets of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric. In research published this year, Ukrainian migrants interviewed by Olena Babakova, a researcher at Warsaw’s Vistula University, identified the 2025 Polish presidential campaign as the period when anti-Ukrainian feeling intensified, as it became a common theme for all parties, not just the far right. Karol Nawrocki, representing the national-conservative camp and who eventually won the presidency, promised legislation that would prioritize Polish citizens over Ukrainians when accessing public services. Rafał Trzaskowski, the liberal candidate, proposed restricting child welfare benefits for Ukrainians. As tensions increased, historical grievances between the countries resurfaced. In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy decided to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during World War II, causing outrage in Poland. Nawrocki responded by withdrawing a state honor awarded to Zelenskyy, further escalating the tensions. “And it's not only negative feelings, Ukrainians really experience hostile conversations and attacks,” Babakova told the AP. According to data from the Polish police, 180 Ukrainian citizens were victims of prejudice-motivated crimes by mid-July, a significant increase compared with 275 for the whole of 2025 and 267 in 2024. In response to multiple media reports of Ukrainians beaten on Polish streets over the summer, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in late July that “we must wage war on violence and hatred.” Help for vulnerable refugees is decreasing The Polish government has been steadily cutting support for Ukrainian refugees, saying that many have stabilized their situation. Poland’s ombudsman has warned that the changes disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups, including single mothers with several children, older people and those with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Because most Ukrainian men of military age, between 23 and 60, are prohibited from leaving the country, single mothers are overrepresented among the refugees. Yuliia Repenko from the Ukrainian House said that her nongovernmental organization, which provides help to Ukrainians, was “increasingly supporting people who are particularly vulnerable to exclusion.” The Polish government has defended its decision to cut back aid to Ukrainian refugees. Katarzyna Nowakowska, Poland's deputy minister for family, labor and social policy, told the AP that the most vulnerable applicants still receive direct help from the state and any other refugees needing support should turn to social workers. As the Polish government has been scaling back its support, international aid has also declined, further limiting options. Data from the U.N. refugee agency shows a steady drop since 2022 in the funding provided by international donors for Ukrainians, with only half the agency’s identified needs financed this year, compared with 94% in 2022. “Financial supporters have moved on from helping Ukrainian refugees, but the war is still ongoing,” said Sonia Novytska, a Martynka helpline worker. “If anything, it has become deadlier since the start.” Martynka received about 1,800 requests for help last year, and staff expect that number to increase, Novytska said. Not only victims of violence contact the helpline now, but also mothers struggling to provide food and shelter for their children. “What Poles need to understand is that we are helping the people that could otherwise become homeless in their neighborhoods, the people who might start abusing substances out of despair they can’t make ends meet,” Podorozhnya said. “Martynka does the job of the Polish state,” she said. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/29/russ.text: A Russian military plane crashed in the far eastern region of Amur on Tuesday, killing six crew members and leaving another injured, the Russian defence ministry said.The Russian defence ministry said the military aircraft went down in an uninhabited area during a training flight and was not carrying ammunition."According to preliminary data, six crew members died, while one was injured and evacuated to a medical facility," the ministry added.According to the Russian state-affiliated media, the crash occurred near the village of Krasnoyarovo shortly after the bomber took off from the Ukrainka air base.Authorities have opened a criminal case and an investigative commission from Russia's Aerospace Forces has been flown to the crash site. Initial assessments suggest the aircraft went down because of a technical malfunction.Unverified videos posted on social media showed what appeared to be flames and smoke rising from the crash site, with booming and crackling sounds in the background.The Tu-95 is a large, nuclear-capable bomber designed in the Soviet Union, first flown in 1952. It is the only turboprop-powered strategic bomber still in operational use.The Ukrainka air base — one of Russia's largest strategic long-range bases — is located in the Seryshevo district of the Amur region, in the country's Far East.In June 2025, it was among the targets of a major operation by Ukraine's security service SBU against Russian military airfields codenamed Spiderweb.In Operation Spiderweb, FPV drones concealed in lorries with remotely opening roofs were used to destroy or damage more than 40 Russian aircraft, including between seven and eight Tu-95s.Russia redeployed the surviving strategic bombers from its European air bases to Ukrainka.

https://www.dw.com/en/north-korea-china-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OGnI The construction of the bridge was completed in 2014 but it remained unused due to lack of connecting roads Image: Ryohei Moriya/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement China and North Korea on Thursday officially opened their most significant land border crossing , aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce after years of strained ties and disruptions. A ceremony was held to launch the New Yalu River Bridge, Chinese state media Xinhua News reported. Meanwhile, China News Service showed visuals of trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea on the bridge, which itself was decorated in flags. The bridge is expected to boost trade and people exchanges between the two nations Image: Pan Yulong/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance Spectators crowded on a road on the Chinese side, in Dandong city, overlooking the ceremony. In Sinuiju city on the North Korean side, work on the approaching road and compound remained unfinished. 'A new chapter' The cable-stayed bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused until now due to lack of connecting roads on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News agency reported. The opening was further delayed by the COVID pandemic which prompted North Korea to close its borders. Train journeys between the East Asian neighbors only restarted in March after six years, but Pyongyang is yet to resume issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, which once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors. The bridge's opening marks the latest sign of warning ties between Beijing and Pyongyang which have conducted two summits between their leaders in the past year. "(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in ​a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency said. He added that the border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and strengthen exchanges between their people. A ceremony was held to mark the bridge's opening more than a decade after it was constructed Image: Pan Yulong/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance A conduit for trade Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told the AFP news agency he expected hundreds of vehicles to cross every day. "The bridge could become a conduit for China's abundant goods and resources to flow into North Korea and give its economy a significant boost," he said. At the same time, experts believe North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China. "The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return ‌to pre-sanctions ​trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But it will help move heavy equipment and raw material North Korea needs for development, he said. China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner despite a series of UN sanctions banning the flow of goods and workers to North Korea over its missile and nuclear weapons program. https://www.politico.eu/article/von-der-.text: BRUSSELS — The EU is expected to prioritize chemicals and industrial machinery in its efforts to protect European industry from Chinese competition, two people with knowledge of the discussion told POLITICO. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was expected to tell EU leaders on Thursday that Brussels is looking at ways to protect the two sectors, the people said on condition of anonymity, with safeguards being the most effective tools currently available to the EU because they can be applied quickly and broadly. Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič struck a deal with Beijing last week that would cap annual imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 units next year — less than half of expected deliveries this year. European governments have called for further sectors to be protected from surging Chinese imports, as the bilateral trade deficit continues to grow. China overtook Germany as the world’s largest machine-tool exporter in 2025. Chinese exports rose 13% to €8.6 billion, while German exports fell 10% to €7 billion, according to Germany’s VDW machine-tool builders’ association. Advertisement Advertisement A similar story has played out in chemicals, where China has doubled its share of the EU’s imports over the past decade, accounting for 18% of the total. Blueprint Speaking in Beijing last week, Šefčovič said the deal on hybrid cars would serve as a “blueprint” for other sectors. A senior Commission official said on Monday that the Commission had also heard complaints about Chinese imports from the wind and furniture industries. EU safeguards on hybrids — which would foresee an import quota and tariffs for volumes above that — should be ready by December, Šefčovič has said, adding that these would comply with the rules of the World Trade Organization. It wasn’t immediately clear whether the proposal for new safeguards on chemicals and machinery had been agreed with Chinese officials. Beijing might very well balk at any new trade restrictions, one analyst warned. A deal on curtailing the surge of imported hybrid vehicles is a one-off that Beijing is unlikely to repeat in other sectors, said Lynn Song, chief economist for China at ING bank. “At some point China would probably end up drawing the line. It’s not likely we’ll see these caps across many products,” he said. “China doesn’t want to set that precedent moving forward.” Advertisement Advertisement Beijing was open to discussing hybrids because of the sheer number of imports this year, Song added. Commission officials have been working on safeguard measures for plastics and epoxy resins, but no investigation, which would precede any trade measures, has been formally launched. The European Commission declined to comment. This report has been updated.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health Centre after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright in Alberta, Canada. Photograph: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP View image in fullscreen Paramedics load an injured person into an ambulance at the Wainwright Health Centre after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright in Alberta, Canada. Photograph: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Canada ‘Serious incident’ at Alberta military base causes deaths and injuries, Canada officials say Patients being taken to hospitals in Edmonton as Wainwright ‘completely overwhelmed’ by number of injuries, local doctor says Guardian staff and agencies Sat 17 Oct 2026 22.50 EDT Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 03.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google People have been killed and injured after an incident at one of Canada’s busiest military training bases in Alberta caused a large fire, Canada’s defence minister said Saturday. “I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” defence minister David McGuinty said at a press conference on Saturday night. McGuinty described the situation at CFB Wainwright as “active and delicate” with the fire being monitored very closely. “I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory”, he said at the press conference, adding that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation. McGuinty did not provide casualty figures or details about what caused the incident. The Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were coordinating the emergency response, he said. The nearby community of Wainwright was providing hospital and firefighting support. Just 14% of Albertans want independence from Canada. Can a conference in a Calgary ballroom change that? Read more A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km northwest of Wainwright, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as Wainwright’s healthcare facilities became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care. “This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra hospital, told CBC news. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.” In an earlier social media post, prime minister Mark Carney said: “A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.” “Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said. The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base’s fence earlier Saturday and was spreading rapidly due to high winds. Firefighters from multiple jurisdictions were responding, and no evacuation order was in effect. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometers an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets. The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel. Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training. The Canadian conservative opposition leader, Pierre Poilievre, said he had spoken with Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire. “Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders. Neither Carney nor Smith provided details about what caused the fire or whether anyone was injured. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-parli.text: STRASBOURG — The European Parliament is launching an internal investigation into a bogus email ostensibly written by a senior European People’s Party lawmaker, apparently attempting to derail a colleague’s bid for a top group post. Andrzej Halicki said the email, received by POLITICO on Thursday , was not written by him and requested that the Parliament ask Belgian authorities to investigate, arguing he is a victim of “shameful allegations based on fake e-mails.” A spokesperson for the Parliament said, “Our services have confirmed that it is not an authentic email. We are in contact with the member concerned to see how this can be best investigated and prevent any further cases like this.” Advertisement Advertisement The email disparaged the work of Portuguese EPP lawmaker Sebastião Bugalho ahead of the EPP’s vice-chair elections. When asked, Bugalho’s office said he “will obviously not comment on forged emails.” Pedro López de Pablo, the EPP’s press director, said: “The group has been informed that there will be an investigation.” The Parliament’s probe was announced by EPP group chair Manfred Weber to all the group’s lawmakers at a closed-door meeting on Monday afternoon, according to four people in the room. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive internal matter. Halicki sent his request for an investigation by Belgian authorities to Parliament President Roberta Metsola on Friday. “As I know, the Parliament immediately reacted, and the investigation has been launched,” he said, referring to the internal probe. The email comes amid a fierce campaign for the EPP’s vice-chair positions, which are to be voted on on Tuesday. Twelve lawmakers, including Bugalho and Halicki, are battling it out for 10 spots. CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misstated Pedro López de Pablo’s role. This article was updated Oct. 19 to correct his title to press director. Advertisement Advertisement
